Research supports metamorphic testing for recommender reliability: a 2024 study tested relations across LibRec, PREA and Surprise, while earlier ML work combined metamorphic relations with mutation analysis. These methods test consistency, which does not establish semantic correctness. Practical inference: candidate permutation equivariance cannot detect a consistently wrong item-ID lookup—scoring embedding row g(item) still preserves candidate order under permutation. Add an independent oracle: hand-constructed, distinct embedding rows and known features, with expected scores calculated directly from the specified scoring equation and an explicit external-ID-to-row table. Avoid reusing production mapping or scoring helpers in expected-value computation. [Recommender study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107410), [ML testing study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3082144/).

Suggested mutation suite: off-by-one IDs, swapped embedding rows, padding-ID aliasing, wrong category mapping, candidate sorting without restoring order, batch-row broadcasting, chunk-boundary omissions, and count-minus-one readout on left-padded histories. Compare singleton, batched and chunked scores for candidate-independent inference in evaluation mode; use numerical tolerances because mathematically equivalent batched computations need not be bitwise identical. These comparisons catch execution-path defects but still miss shared mapping errors, so retain the independent fixture oracle. Track which test kills each mutant; distinguish surviving faults from genuinely equivalent changes. Equivalence depends on the observable contract: a positive score scaling preserves rankings while changing raw scores. Mutation-testing research cautions that mutant design and interpretation determine what adequacy claims actually mean. [PyTorch numerical guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/numerical_accuracy.html), [Mutation-testing reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01341).
